examples.question_text: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=8t-6$ m/s² and velocity $v(2)=9$ m/s. Find its velocity as a function of time.
A particle has acceleration $a(t)=12\cos(4t)$ m/s², where $t$ is in seconds and angles are in radians. Its initial velocity is $-1$ m/s. Find $v(t)$.
A particle has velocity $v(t)=6t^2-4t+3$ m/s. Its displacement is $8$ m when $t=1$ s. Find its displacement function.
A particle has acceleration $a(t)=8t-4$ m/s², with $v(0)=3$ m/s and $x(0)=-2$ m. Find its velocity and displacement functions.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\int(8t-4)\,dt\\&=4t^2-4t+C\end{align*}$
Using $v(0)=3$ gives $C=3$, so $v(t)=4t^2-4t+3$ m/s.
$\begin{align*}x(t)&=\int(4t^2-4t+3)\,dt\\&=\frac43t^3-2t^2+3t+D\end{align*}$
Using $x(0)=-2$ gives $D=-2$, so $x(t)=\frac43t^3-2t^2+3t-2$ m.

examples.question_text: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=18t-8$ m/s². Its displacement is $2$ m at $t=0$ and $10$ m at $t=2$ s. Find its displacement function.
A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^3+3t+2$ metres. Find its displacement from $t=1$ to $t=3$ seconds, first using the displacement function and then using a definite integral of velocity.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}x(1)&=1+3+2\\&=6\text{ m}\\x(3)&=27+9+2\\&=38\text{ m}\end{align*}$
The displacement is $x(3)-x(1)=38-6=32$ m.
Differentiating gives $v(t)=3t^2+3$ m/s. Equivalently:
$\begin{align*}\int_1^3v(t)\,dt&=\int_1^3(3t^2+3)\,dt\\&=[t^3+3t]_1^3\\&=36-4\\&=32\text{ m}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text:
A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^3-12t^2+36t+1$ metres for $0\le t\le7$ seconds.
(a) Find its velocity and acceleration.
(b) Find when it changes direction.
(c) Find its displacement and distance travelled over the interval.
(d) Find the open intervals during which it is speeding up.
examples.solution_text:
(a)
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\frac{dx}{dt}\\&=3t^2-24t+36\\&=3(t-2)(t-6)\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}a(t)&=\frac{dv}{dt}\\&=6t-24\\&=6(t-4)\end{align*}$
Velocity is measured in m/s and acceleration in m/s².
(b) Setting $v(t)=0$ gives $t=2$ or $t=6$. Velocity is positive for $0\le t<2$, negative for $2<t<6$, and positive for $6<t\le7$. It changes sign at both zeros, so the particle changes direction at $2$ s and $6$ s.
(c) The displacements at the endpoints and turning times are $x(0)=1$, $x(2)=33$, $x(6)=1$ and $x(7)=8$ metres.
$\begin{align*}\text{Displacement}&=x(7)-x(0)\\&=8-1\\&=7\text{ m}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}\text{Distance}&=|33-1|+|1-33|+|8-1|\\&=32+32+7\\&=71\text{ m}\end{align*}$
(d) Acceleration is negative before $t=4$ and positive after $t=4$. Velocity and acceleration are both negative on $2<t<4$ and both positive on $6<t<7$. The particle is speeding up on these intervals. On $4<t<6$, positive acceleration accompanies negative velocity, so it is slowing down.

examples.question_text: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=12t-30$ m/s², with $v(0)=18$ m/s and $x(0)=0$ m. Find the distance it travels in the first $5$ seconds.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\int(12t-30)\,dt\\&=6t^2-30t+C\end{align*}$
Using $v(0)=18$ gives $C=18$.
$\begin{align*}x(t)&=\int(6t^2-30t+18)\,dt\\&=2t^3-15t^2+18t+D\end{align*}$
Using $x(0)=0$ gives $D=0$.
At rest:
$\begin{align*}6t^2-30t+18&=0\\t^2-5t+3&=0\\t&=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{13}}2\end{align*}$
Both times lie inside $0<t<5$. Write $r=\frac{5-\sqrt{13}}2$ and $s=\frac{5+\sqrt{13}}2$. Velocity is positive before $r$, negative between $r$ and $s$, and positive after $s$.
At either root, $t^2=5t-3$ and $t^3=22t-15$, so:
$\begin{align*}x(t)&=2(22t-15)-15(5t-3)+18t\\&=15-13t\end{align*}$
Thus $x(r)=\frac{-35+13\sqrt{13}}2$, $x(s)=\frac{-35-13\sqrt{13}}2$, $x(0)=0$ and $x(5)=-35$ metres.
$\begin{align*}\text{Distance}&=|x(r)|+|x(s)-x(r)|+|-35-x(s)|\\&=\frac{-35+13\sqrt{13}}2+13\sqrt{13}+\frac{-35+13\sqrt{13}}2\\&=26\sqrt{13}-35\text{ m}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=2te^{-t}$ metres for $t\ge0$ seconds. Show that it changes direction exactly once and find its displacement then.
examples.solution_text:
Using the product rule:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=2e^{-t}-2te^{-t}\\&=2(1-t)e^{-t}\end{align*}$
Since $e^{-t}>0$, velocity is zero only at $t=1$. It is positive for $0\le t<1$ and negative for $t>1$. The particle therefore changes direction exactly once, at $1$ s.
$\begin{align*}x(1)&=2e^{-1}\\&=\frac2e\text{ m}\end{align*}$

examples.derivation: Integrating 8t−6 gives 4t²−6t+C. At t=2, 9=4+C, so C=5 and v(t)=4t²−6t+5 m/s.
Integrating 12cos(4t) gives 3sin(4t)+C. The initial velocity gives C=−1, hence v(t)=3sin(4t)−1 m/s. Differentiation recovers the given acceleration.
Integrating velocity gives x(t)=2t³−2t²+3t+C. Since x(1)=3+C=8, C=5.
Integrating acceleration and applying v(0)=3 gives v(t)=4t²−4t+3. Integrating again and applying x(0)=−2 gives x(t)=(4/3)t³−2t²+3t−2 m.
Two integrations give v(t)=9t²−8t+C and x(t)=3t³−4t²+Ct+D. The first displacement condition gives D=2; the second gives 10=24−16+2C+2, hence C=0.
The endpoint positions are x(1)=6 and x(3)=38, giving displacement 32 m. Differentiating gives v(t)=3t²+3; its integral from 1 to 3 is [t³+3t]₁³=36−4=32 m.

Differentiation gives v=3(t−2)(t−6) and a=6(t−4). Velocity has signs positive, negative, positive across t=2 and t=6, confirming both direction changes. Positions at t=0,2,6,7 are 1,33,1,8 m. Displacement is 7 m and distance is 32+32+7=71 m. Velocity and acceleration share signs on (2,4) and (6,7), the requested open speeding-up intervals.

The initial conditions give v=6t²−30t+18 and x=2t³−15t²+18t. Velocity zeros are r=(5−√13)/2 and s=(5+√13)/2, both within (0,5), with signs positive, negative, positive. At either zero, t²=5t−3 and t³=22t−15, so x=15−13t. Therefore x(r)=(−35+13√13)/2, x(s)=(−35−13√13)/2 and x(5)=−35. Adding the three absolute position changes gives 26√13−35 m.

The product rule gives v=2(1−t)e^(−t). The exponential factor is strictly positive, so the sole velocity zero is t=1, with positive velocity before and negative velocity after. The displacement then is x(1)=2/e m.

The plotted velocity is v(t)=(t-2)(t-6). Its zeros are t=2 and t=6. The factors have opposite signs precisely for 2<t<6, so velocity is negative on that interval. The vertex is (4,-4), and both endpoint velocities are 12 m/s, consistent with the plotted bounds. The solution marks the correct intercepts and highlights exactly the negative-velocity segment. Both coordinate annotations now use south anchors with 3 mm upward offsets, separating them from the time-axis tick-label row without changing mathematical content.

The plotted displacement is x(t)=6t-t^2. Independently differentiating gives v(t)=6-2t, which vanishes at t=3; x(3)=9 m. Factoring x(t)=t(6-t) gives origin times t=0 and t=6. Their velocities are 6 and -6 m/s respectively, so neither is a rest time. The solution's horizontal line at x=9 is tangent at (3,9), and all three marked coordinates are correct. The intercept annotations now sit 3 mm above the axis. The time-axis title is anchored at the right edge on the zero-displacement row, then shifted downward 8 mm, separating its intended position from the (6,0) annotation.
